title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education from 2010 to 2020
authors: Xuesong Zhai, Xiaoyan Chu, Ching Sing Chai, Morris Siu–Yung Jong, Andreja Istenič Starčič, Michael Spector, et al.
explain_beginner: This paper looked at 100 studies about artificial intelligence in education, published between 2010 and 2020. The authors sorted the research into three groups: tools that classify or recommend things, tools that give feedback or adapt to learners, and tools that involve emotions, role play, immersive learning, or games. They found the field is moving toward more personal and interactive learning. They also warn that problems like misuse of AI, changing roles for teachers and students, and ethical concerns matter just as much as the technology. This helps readers understand both the promise and the risks of AI in classrooms.
explain_business: This review of 100 papers from 2010 to 2020 shows that AI in education has shifted from simple sorting and recommending toward adaptive, immersive, and gamified learning. For leaders, the key message is that the technology alone is not enough. Inappropriate use, changing roles of teachers and students, and social and ethical concerns are just as important as the tools. This informs decisions about investing in AI for training or education, and it argues for pairing technology adoption with clear policies on ethics, teacher support, and student roles rather than treating AI as a purely technical purchase.
explain_practitioner: The authors performed a content analysis of 100 papers from the Social Sciences Citation Index education category, covering 2010 to 2020. Of these, 63 were empirical papers containing 74 studies, and 37 were analytic. Research questions were grouped into three layers: development (classification, matching, recommendation, deep learning), application (feedback, reasoning, adaptive learning), and integration (affection computing, role playing, immersive learning, gamification). Suggested future trends include the Internet of Things, swarm intelligence, deep learning, neuroscience, and assessment of AI in education. Reported challenges include inappropriate use of AI techniques, shifting teacher and student roles, and social and ethical issues.
